title: Longest Common Subpath
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every candidate directly versus binary search on the length with a rolling hash and set intersection.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: There are n cities and m friends, where each friend's road trip is recorded as a path, an array of city labels visited in order. Return the length of the longest contiguous stretch of cities that appears, in the exact same order, as a contiguous subarray within every single friend's path.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

There are n cities and m friends, where each friend's road trip is recorded as a path, an array of city labels visited in order. Return the length of the longest contiguous stretch of cities that appears, in the exact same order, as a contiguous subarray within every single friend's path.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Longest Shared Stretch of a Group Road Trip
blocks.text: Like comparing several friends' separately recorded road trip logs and looking for the longest unbroken stretch of towns that every single friend drove through, in the same order, at some point during their own trip.

blocks.caption: Find the longest contiguous stretch of cities common to every single path

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples

blocks.text: Edge case: paths = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
These two paths share no cities at all, so there is no common subpath of any positive length, giving 0.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask whether checking every possible length independently is really necessary, or whether the lengths themselves relate to each other in a useful way.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force generates every candidate subarray from just the first path and directly searches for it inside every other path, which is correct but treats every candidate length as an entirely separate problem.

Observation 2: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array and Sqrt(x) already showed that a monotonic yes or no question, true up to some threshold and false beyond it, can be searched with binary search instead of checking every value individually; here, if a common subpath of length L exists, one of any shorter length trivially exists too (just trim it), giving exactly that monotonic shape.

Observation 3: Distinct Echo Substrings and Find Substring with Given Hash Value already showed that a rolling hash represents every fixed length window as a single comparable number, computed incrementally instead of rebuilt from scratch; the same idea extends here to testing "is length L achievable" directly, by computing every path's set of length L window hashes and intersecting those sets across all paths.

Observation 4: Tracing paths equal to [[1,2,3,4],[2,3,4,5],[0,2,3,9]] for length 2 confirms it, the surviving hash set narrows from two candidates down to just one as each additional path's hash set is intersected in, proving length 2 is achievable, while binary search on top of this feasibility check converges on the true answer, 2, without ever testing every length one by one.

Recognizing that subpath feasibility is monotonic in length, and that a rolling hash can test any one length's feasibility quickly across all paths at once, is what turns this problem into a binary search wrapped around a rolling hash set intersection.
6. Brute Force Solution

Take every possible contiguous subarray of the first path as a candidate, and for each one, directly search whether it appears as a contiguous subarray inside every other path, keeping track of the longest candidate that succeeds everywhere.
Step by step algorithm

items: Generate every contiguous subarray of the first path as a candidate.
For each candidate, directly search for it inside every other path using a straightforward subarray search.
Keep the longest candidate that is found in every single path.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Only the first path is used to generate candidates, since any common subpath must, in particular, appear somewhere within it.
Each candidate is checked directly against every remaining path using a straightforward element by element subarray search.
Only candidates confirmed present in every single path are considered for the running best length.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every candidate subpath from the first path is directly checked against every other path, so the true longest common subpath is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: extremely slow, roughly the cube of the path length times the number of paths, since there are a quadratic number of candidates, each needing a linear search through every other path.
Space: O(path length), for each candidate subarray being built and compared.

Limitation: this approach only ever generates candidates from the first path, and checks each one with a slow direct search, when the actual structure of the problem (a length threshold that is easy to check and monotonic) suggests a much faster overall strategy.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it generates a quadratic number of candidate subarrays and searches for each one directly, never exploiting any relationship between different candidate lengths.

What recognizing monotonicity fixes: since a common subpath of length L implies one of any shorter length also exists, testing feasibility only needs to happen at a binary search style handful of lengths, not every one individually.

What a rolling hash fixes at each tested length: representing every length L window across all paths as a hash value turns "does a common window exist" into a fast set intersection instead of a slow direct search.

The core idea: binary search on the candidate length, and at each length tested, use rolling hashes and set intersection across all paths to check feasibility quickly.

Notice that if a common subpath of some length L exists across all paths, then a common subpath of any shorter length also trivially exists (just trim it), so the question "is there a common subpath of length L" becomes true for all lengths up to some maximum and false beyond it, a textbook monotonic condition perfect for binary search. For each candidate length tested during the binary search, compute the set of rolling hash values of every length L window in the first path, then for every subsequent path, compute its own set of length L window hashes and keep only the hashes that survive in every path so far. If any hash value survives all paths, that length is achievable.
9. Optimized Solution
Binary search over the candidate length, using a rolling hash and set intersection to test feasibility of each length quickly.
Dry run checking whether length 2 is feasible, for paths = [[1, 2, 3, 4], [2, 3, 4, 5], [0, 2, 3, 9]]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Length 2 window hashes for path 0","hash of [1,2], hash of [2,3], hash of [3,4]"],["Length 2 window hashes for path 1","hash of [2,3], hash of [3,4], hash of [4,5]"],["Intersect path 0 and path 1 hash sets","hash of [2,3] and hash of [3,4] survive"],["Length 2 window hashes for path 2","hash of [0,2], hash of [2,3], hash of [3,9]"],["Intersect the running set with path 2's set","only hash of [2,3] survives"],["At least one hash survives every path","length 2 is feasible"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: binary search the length, testing feasibility with rolling hashes and set intersection

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because a hash value survives intersection across every path only if the exact same length L window truly occurs in all of them, so a non empty surviving set after checking all paths is proof that a genuine common subpath of that length exists, and combined with the proven monotonicity of feasibility, binary search over the length converges correctly on the true maximum in logarithmic steps.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The intersection of surviving hashes becomes empty partway through checking the paths","The function returns false immediately, this length is infeasible","Binary search narrows toward shorter candidate lengths"],["At least one hash survives intersection with every single path","The function returns true, this length is feasible","Binary search narrows toward longer candidate lengths, remembering this length as a valid answer"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((total number of elements across all paths) times log of the shortest path length), since each binary search step processes every path once using rolling hashes.
Space: O(total number of elements across all paths), for the hash sets built at each step.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Lengths Tested","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (every candidate from path 0)","Roughly cubic in path length times number of paths","O(path length)","Every possible length independently","Correct, but far too slow for real input sizes."],["Optimized (binary search plus rolling hash)","O(total elements times log of shortest path length)","O(total elements)","A logarithmic number of lengths, via binary search","The expected answer, combining two techniques already seen separately."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The two ideas that make this problem tractable are recognizing the monotonic "is length L achievable" property that enables binary search, and using a rolling hash to represent every window of a fixed length as a single comparable value, so that checking whether any common window exists across all paths becomes a fast set intersection instead of a slow direct search.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to intersect the running set of surviving hashes progressively with each path, instead comparing only the first and last paths and missing a path in between that breaks the common subpath.

Using a single hash function without any collision safeguard on a problem with adversarial test data, where a more careful implementation would use double hashing or verify a hash match with a direct comparison.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explain the binary search framing explicitly before diving into the rolling hash mechanics, since recognizing "is a common subpath of length L achievable" as a monotonic yes or no question is the single biggest conceptual leap in this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every possible length", think: binary search on the length, since feasibility is monotonic.
If the interviewer says "how do you check one length quickly across many paths", think: a rolling hash set per path, intersected progressively across all of them.
If the interviewer says "what if a hash collision occurs", think: use a large prime modulus, or double hashing, or verify a surviving hash with a direct comparison for extra safety.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why is "a common subpath of length L exists" a monotonic property, and why does that specifically enable binary search?
Why must the surviving hash set be intersected progressively with every path, rather than just checked against the first and last?
How would you adapt this approach to find the actual common subpath itself, not just its length?
How would this approach change if paths could be updated dynamically between queries?
How would you extend this technique to find the longest common subpath shared by at least some fraction of the paths, rather than all of them?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array and Sqrt(x), whose binary search on a monotonic yes or no condition is the exact same framing applied here to subpath length feasibility.
Distinct Echo Substrings and Find Substring with Given Hash Value, whose rolling hash techniques are extended here to compare windows across multiple separate arrays at once via set intersection.
Any "find the maximum value satisfying a monotonic condition" problem, where binary searching the answer itself, paired with a fast feasibility check, is the standard combination to reach for.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: roughly cubic time in path length times the number of paths, O(path length) space per candidate. Optimized (binary search plus rolling hash): O((total elements across all paths) times log of the shortest path length) time, O(total elements across all paths) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: binary search over the candidate length, testing feasibility at each length with a rolling hash and set intersection across all paths.

Core Idea: subpath feasibility is monotonic in length, so binary searching the length, paired with a rolling hash set intersection to test each candidate length quickly across every path, finds the true maximum efficiently.
Time: roughly cubic in path length for the brute force, O(total elements times log of the shortest path length) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(path length) for the brute force, O(total elements across all paths) for the optimized approach.

Most Important Observation: two previously seen techniques, binary search on a monotonic condition and a rolling hash for fast window comparison, combine directly to solve a problem neither could solve as efficiently alone.

Interview Difficulty: recognizing the monotonic structure is the key conceptual leap; correctly implementing the rolling hash and progressive set intersection across many paths is the harder implementation detail.
One line memory trick: binary search the length, and test each one with rolling hash sets intersected across every path.
